utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made when you commenced your evidence, it still applies. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Covic. I am about to pick up where I left off last night. I will be asking you a number of questions about Vukovar just before the clashes broke out. In answer to one of my questions yesterday, I believe you said that there had been an incident at Bogdanovci where the local population had stopped a JNA convoy from passing through the village. Was anything like this happening in Vukovar itself at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one such incident in Vukovar itself. After the crime that had occurred in Borovo Selo the tanks were on their way to Borovo Selo and they said that they would try to protect peace. However, what they eventually did was quite the opposite. They positioned themselves between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje as some sort of a barricade. I'm not sure if I should put this in a different way, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question was about any incidents that were similar to the one at Bogdanovci that you described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You described that the JNA positioned itself between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this not a way to prevent clashes from breaking out? If I'm not mistaken, Borovo Selo was predominantly Serb and Borovo Naselje was predominantly Croat.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not what they were doing because there was still sporadic firing from Borovo Selo, and they did not react to that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you are now telling us is your own personal knowledge, or is this something based on hearsay?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned from our electricians who had gone to Borovo and some of them had gone to the technology centre near the airfield at Borovo Naselje. They said they had been forced to take cover quickly because shooting was constant from Borovo Selo. They were firing at Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber and for the benefit of everyone else, I'm talking now about this place between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje. In order to get there, you would have had to pass through Borovo Naselje first, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you had to take a round about route through Luzac. If you're familiar with the Vukovar area, then you should understand which route I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm sure that you know where the JNA barracks was. At this point in time were you aware of the fact that the electricity and water supplies to the barracks had been cut off?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been no power cuts until the 24th of August anywhere in town, when following some massive shelling of the entire town there was a large-scale power cut and electricity was not restored until Vukovar eventually fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there were no power cuts, that the electricity and water supplies of the barracks were never cut at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the barracks or any other part of town for that matter. I'm certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about the fact that you were a reserve JNA captain first class. That was your rank. Several questions I would like to ask you about that. As a reserve officer, did you keep a uniform at home?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. We did not have reserve officers' uniforms. It was only whenever we were called up to serve with the reserve forces. These would usually be 10-day stints. The recruitment office would provide those for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that at least some of the reserve officers did keep their own uniforms at home at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they did, but I can't be certain about this. I can't answer this question. I can't answer this question. I didn't go to their homes to see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your son was mobilised, or perhaps he joined of his own free will, the National Guards Corps in July 1991. Is that a fair assessment of what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son was indeed a defender of Vukovar. The manner in which he joined is less important. I do not wish to go into that now. It was about his feelings and this applied to everybody else in Vukovar. They stood up to defend their city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say "they stood up to defend their city." From whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the JNA, from Seselj's men, from the Chetniks. Near Borovo Naselje, there was a group of Arkan's men, and some TO people, local Serbs, who joined forces with the JNA in a bid to occupy Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that you mention this, can you please tell me how exactly did the JNA intend to go about occupying Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By force. Again, I have to go back to the 24th. The entire town was heavily shelled on that day. There was firing from all sorts of weapons, howitzers, mortars, guns, tanks of all sorts and kinds. The heavy shelling was actually done by planes right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We'll get to that, but there's something I need to ask you first. I'm not sure if I understand you correctly. You said you did not wish to answer my question about your son being mobilised or joining the national guards forces of his own free will. Was that what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear about the purpose of your question or what it has to do with my testimony at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know if all able-bodied men, all men fit for military service who were in Vukovar at the time were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was mobilised in Vukovar at the time. They all volunteered. They all volunteered to become Vukovar's defenders. It was all done on a voluntary basis, and there was no mandatory mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What if someone refused to become a volunteer, as you say? Would such a person have been likely to encounter any problems on account of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think there would have been any problems with that. There were some people who were indirectly involved, but this was probably due to their age or poor health. These people did their best to try to help the defenders by providing any food that was available. It was a difficult time for us and both food and water were in short supply. That's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about your son? I'm not sure what age he was at the time. Had he already served his military term with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had. At this time he was a student. He was attending university, and unfortunately, because of what started happening in Vukovar, he could no longer continue his studies in Osijek. He had to continue in Zagreb later on and so on and so forth. I don't think it's very important for us to dwell on this topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that Croatian defence forces, as you called them, shot down two planes over Vukovar. Are you certain about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain about this. But I didn't say two, I said about 20 in all likelihood. Throughout the entire time of Vukovar's defence and we're looking at three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is decidedly not what you said yesterday. You did not specify that 20 plane where is shot down. I am certain, however, that you said that two planes were shot down in a single day. I assume that must have been the first day of Vukovar's defence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is an entirely different issue. And what you are putting to me is quite correct, it was the very first day of the shelling of Vukovar, and on that day two planes were shot down, and this is something that I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That precisely is my question. How do you know this? Did you personally witness these planes being shot down?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them when they were hit and I saw them fall down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me where this happened, where were they hit and where did they eventually land or crash?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in a neighbourhood that was near Brsadin. There is with a grain silo there, and one of our defence units were was stationed in the silo and that's where the planes were shot at from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the sequence. Were these two planes shot down at the same time, or was there a time-lag between the two planes being shot down?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very short interval between the two planes being shot down. These planes were shelling Borovo Naselje for the most part, and that was the reason that fire was returned from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you certain about those two planes shelling Vukovar on that day or were they merely flying over Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were shelling, that's for sure, especially Borovo Naselje. And that's why fire was returned from that silo just outside the town near Brsadin. The area is called Borovo Naselje. Those people were trying to defend themselves to protect themselves from the planes and that's why they fired at them and eventually shot them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe you said yesterday that the planes were shot down by hand-held rocket launchers. Did I hear you correctly or do you have a different explanation now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not something I personally witnessed. I made an assumption that this was the case. I knew a thing or two about the weapons those people had. But it's possible that before the attack on Vukovar and the aggression against Croatia at the Borovo factory they kept a number of anti-aircraft guns. I'm not sure if they were using those or not. I simply don't know, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you were an eye-witness, perhaps you could tell us about the altitude those planes were flying at at the time they were shot down, roughly speaking, of course?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really difficult to say. I suppose the altitude might have been about 1.000 metres. Probably not more. Perhaps lower. I just saw them being shot down and they were falling somewhere near the Danube area. I'm not sure where they eventually crashed. Maybe that was over in Backa, but I think you would be better placed to answer that than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were a reserve officer and you completed your military training in Zadar. There is military airfield there, I think. Can you perhaps tell us about the type of plane that was shot down?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For as long as I was in Zadar, I never went to the airfield. When we had target practice, it was usually carried out somewhere between Zadar and the oldest Croatian city, the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: May I therefore conclude that you do not know anything about the type of plane in question?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about the 24th of August as the day when this occurred. So this was perhaps on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. This was on the 23rd. It was on the 23rd that Borovo Naselje suffered the heaviest shelling. The next day, the 24th [realtime transcript read in error "14th"], the entire town was shelled. There wasn't much difference really from there on. Shells continued to rain down on us every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There is something in the transcript on page 8, line 9. The date reflected there is the 14th, whereas it should be the 24th, because that's what the witness said, that the shelling began on the 24th, one day after the planes had been shot down. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Borovo Naselje is part of Vukovar, and that is crystal clear. What I'm saying is that on the 24th all the other parts of town came under attack and suffered heavy shelling. Very heavy shelling. There is something important that I need to point out about the 23rd. Many of the children who had been vacationing somewhere along the coast returned to Vukovar. And we see what happened to them the next day upon their return. I'm not sure how many of them survived. That is why I remember the 24th with particular clarity. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the planes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to say something about the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So we agree that this was on the 23rd. What time of day, and what was your vantage point as you were watching this going on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably late afternoon, and I'm not sure why you wish to know about my vantage point or where I was physically located as I was watching this going on. I don't think that matters at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to try to answer all my questions to the best of your ability and recollection.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. But if one of your questions is an unpleasant one, then I regret to say that I should inform everyone here in the courtroom I'm likely to refuse to answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why would that be an unpleasant question, sir? I'm asking you about where you were standing as this was going on. I'm just trying to assess the credibility of your testimony here as well the truthfulness of what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that I'm telling the truth, and I'll always be telling the truth. I'm not in least ashamed of anything that I have said because I know that I have been telling the truth throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'll give this question another go. Will you please tell us where were you at the time the two planes were shot down? Where were you watching from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would you want to know that? Let me ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I am no position to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. It would greatly assist the Chamber if you would just answer the questions that are put to you because we were not there, you were. And we've got to try and see what happened through your eyes, you see. The three Judges here don't have the advantage of your knowledge of these events. But we've got to try and understand in the end what happened. And it certainly will help us to know how it was you were able to see these things. If there are questions that come up that are particularly personally distressing, do let us know and we'll try and find a way around them. But if you wouldn't mind telling us where you were on this occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this occasion I was in our neighbourhood, which is on an elevation, a small hill, you might say, a hillock. Where the planes were shot down the distance would have been no further than two kilometres as the crow flies, and everybody saw this. We were talking about it, and we were in actual fact quite happy that our defenders had managed to ward off those first two planes that were shelling Borovo Naselje quite heavily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Mr. Covic, you and a number of other people were watching this. You were in an open area at a time when these planes were shelling Vukovar. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just another question about this, since today you brought this up for the first time. You said that in your estimate a total of about 20 planes were shot down throughout the duration of the clashes in Vukovar. You have provided a very detailed explanation. What about the remaining planes in addition to those first two planes? What do you know about those?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that when attacking they were usually arriving from the opposite direction, and flying across the Danube. When the planes were shot down probably those who were carrying out the shelling to begin with, they were reckoned that if they were hit and if they were to crash they would probably prefer to crash somewhere across the Danube, and probably they did. My own neighbourhood was probably shelled twice. There were a number of houses that were hit and razed to the ground by the shells. Thank God, however, we ourselves and the defenders were hiding elsewhere at the time in cellars, away from that neighbourhood and nobody was really hit. Some people were slightly injured at worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, can I ask you to please try not to stray too far from my question? In answer to my previous question you said you saw those planes being shot down for the most part. I took that to mean that you saw other planes being shot down. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it in the same way as the first time when you observed it, were you at more or less the same location or were you in the street or what?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, not -- not exactly the same place. This is the same neighbourhood in an area of about two, 300 metres, a perimeter like that, and I was in the same neighbourhood. I can't exactly remember what part of it, whether I was five houses down the road or whatever. It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, but my question was something else, and you answered it. Thank you. This shooting down of planes and the first two that you mentioned in particular, was it a widely known fact in Vukovar, or was it a kind of secret information that was not forwarded to anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't secret. Many people witnessed it. And those who didn't who were hiding in cellars underground to save their lives were certainly told about it, so everybody knew and everybody was pleased that our defenders were managing to defend the city, even from war planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We're still talking about the same day, the 23rd of August. Was there a front line at the fair where your son was and you were involved with that fair as well, were you at that front line at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, of course. But the defenders were closer to the barracks and closer to the Petrova Gora neighbourhood and in that part of town it's called the Radnicka Street, and it was in that part of town that the defenders were facing the attackers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one point about the shelling, I don't seem to recall you mentioning that, but it is referred to in your statement. Apart from planes, where else did the shelling come from? We're talking about the 24th, and you mentioned significant shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the shelling on the 24th came from the barracks, from the Petrova Gora neighbourhood, where quite a few local Serbs used to live, and from Borovo Naselje, from Borovo Selo, and from the direction of Trpinja. From those directions, that's where most of the shelling came from in the beginning, in the first few days. As to anything else, in case you want to ask any other questions, I will be glad to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking you this, because in your statement -- or, rather, let me ask you this first: Is it correct that you made a statement to the Prosecution in 2003? Did you make a statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Because what it says here, and I'm going to read this part out to you, the subtitle is the shelling of Vukovar, and you can tell me whether this is indeed your statement of not. You most certainly have it in front of you. In case you do, could you look at page 4 where it reads after the bombing of JNA planes you said that Vukovar was being shelled from across the Danube and the vessels on the Danube. And you never mentioned what you've mentioned now, but you said that the shelling had come from across the Danube and the vessels on the Danube. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say this. We were talking about the shelling throughout this three-month period, and so I mentioned all the various directions from where the shelling came from. And now you're asking me about the first few days. So that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: First of all, your statement refers to the shelling on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If the witness is going to be referred to parts of the statement, in my submission, it's only fair he should see the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Moore. You want it on the screen, Mr. Domazet, or in paper form?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my understanding was that the witness did have the statement in front of him, and that he could take a look at page 4 of the B/C/S version of the document, the paragraph that refers to the shelling of Vukovar. If the usher would like to give the document to the witness, we could give it to him, or help him out in case he is unable to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is in the first line on page 4. It says JNA shelled Vukovar from the area across the Danube as well as the JNA vessels along the Danube behind the Vukovar ada.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does say so in my statement, that's correct, because I'm a reserve officer in the artillery. Since I was often invited to participate in reserve officer's training exercises for 10 days at a time, I did learn quite a few things, and amongst other things I was able to recognise the type of shell, whether it was a mortar, a howitzer, or whatever. And I could explain it to the defenders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it assists the Court, the witness has the copy of his statement in of course a file that has been closed. Now I'm quite happy for it to be shown on the computer screen. I don't whether my learned friends are happy for the hard copy to be shown to him. There is always a danger he will see other parts. I'm quite flexible in relation to the way it's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be helpful first if the document could come on to the screens in the available languages; and secondly it would be helpful to be sure that the witness has the statement and not some other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm not going to keep dwelling on this, Your Honour. I believe that the answer has been given. Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talked about the participation of the defenders of Vukovar yesterday, you mentioned a group of police officers from Zadar who reinforced ranks of the defenders.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm still grateful to them, even now. There were the true defenders of our city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It seems to me that you had also mentioned a group of police officers from Varazdin. Were there any police officers from Varazdin as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that line, front line at the fair, were there any members of the HOS? You know what I have in mind, the Paragas [phoen] forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of the HOS in Vukovar only for a few days. And then they went to Bogdanovci, and that's where they acted as defenders and that's where they did most of their work up until the fall of that town on the 11th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say a few days, what few days do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact dates, but I believe it was about 10 days, roughly speaking, after the 24th of August. And then they moved to Bogdanovci to defend Bogdanovci, since they were very few defenders there, and their needs were greater. So that's why they went to Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Alenka Mirkovic? Who was she; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It rings a bell, but I can't recall who it was. And also considering my cerebral lesions, it is a bit difficult for me to remember people if I simply hear their names. If I see people, I tend to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I reminded you that she was a journalist from Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, you've reminded now. Now I remember, yes. She used to work for Radio Vukovar. She was the journalist. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that she was writing about HOS and the participation of their forces in the defence of Sajmiste? She described them as the heros of Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She wrote a book, actually, and I read the book and we are very grateful to her because she gave a very fine description of everything and everything was very accurate. And I would really like the book to be submitted here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, do you know what the term "osa 1," "osa 2," "osa 3" meant?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Osa" meant nothing to us. Maybe within the JNA? No, I don't know. May I ask a question, actually? I would like Your Honours to allow me to have a short break now. Because I'm getting a bit tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Given your situation, we will adjourn now, but it will be for 20 minutes. We will resume at 20 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I seek the Court's leave to clarify through the witness service if there are any problems in relation to this witness? I meant health-wise in relation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh. During the adjournment, I think that might be something the Defence would be happy with. It will be for our own convenience and everybody's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. --- Break taken at 3.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session to clarify certain matters? And the Defence have indeed suggested we go into private session to talk about the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, are you familiar with the Stjepan Sapanc school in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the Stjepan Sapanc school. Do you want me to tell you where it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is next to the park near the medical centre, opposite the medical centre, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the course of this war, and for the most time that these battles were taking place, was this on the front line as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was close to the front line, and that school was terribly damaged. It was destroyed. But now, thank God, it's been restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the course of the war, did you visit the school?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had never been there. I was in my neighbourhood throughout, and I was close to our boys from the neighbourhood and the surrounding areas, the boys that I knew better, and that we assisted a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And according to what you have just said, may I conclude that this front line where your son was and where you spent most of your time was slightly further away from that school?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a couple of kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talked about the weapons held by the defenders of Vukovar, you talked about various things, but you also mentioned some implements which were manufactured at the Borovo plant, and most of those who had the opportunity to use those tools praised them a great deal. Considering that you were an artillery officer, you might know a little bit more about that and you could perhaps tell us what implements we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself cannot tell you what weapons those were. I only found out about that after the camp. And when we were in Zagreb as refugees, certain individuals who were involved in the manufacturing of all that told me about how they helped the defenders in that way. But I had never seen those weapons, and I was rather surprised, and I was very pleased to hear that they found a way of helping the defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the examination-in-chief yesterday you reiterated something which you had mentioned before. Following a question from my learned colleague, you said that you often heard megaphones or loud-speakers and there were speeches by Vojislav Seselj himself. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you said that he himself was the speaker. He was probably delivering those speeches from the other side of the front line where he could do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you want me to try and tell you what route he used to take. And the defenders and the people who were closer to the front line explained to me that he would move from the barracks to the Petrova Gora neighbourhood, and that street is certainly at least a kilometre long, and he was driving in a tank along that road, and he was calling for all of us, as he called us Ustashas, to give ourselves up, otherwise we would be killed, and he was addressing the entire city of Vukovar, and obviously at Borovo Naselje they knew it before, but on that occasion we heard for the first time that our famous fighter and defender Blago Zadar had been killed. We heard it from him, and he was threatening that the same fate would befall all of us unless we gave ourselves up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have frequently did this happen? You did say a thing or two about that in your statement, so I would like you to tell us now. How often was this the case? I mean Vojislav Seselj speaking over the PA system.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too often, but probably four or five times, at least. We recognised the voice, because we had heard him previously before the war on both TV and the radio. We immediately identified Seselj's voice. Later on we found out who he had been staying with, where he had been sleeping at the Tehnostan director's and manager's place. That was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on your answer, can we agree that you are absolutely certain that this person speaking was Vojislav Seselj and no one else and that it wasn't less than four or five times that he spoke in this way, on four or five occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am positive myself. And whenever I talk to other people they all confirmed identifying Seselj's voice. I'm not sure if I should add this, but my wife too was very explicit about recognising Seselj's voice, as well as all the other civilians there. No one ever thought about any other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that this was how you found out that Blago Zadar had been killed, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me more specifically who he was and how he was killed? Was it outside of Vukovar or in Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Vukovar itself. First of all, we learned about this while we were listening to Seselj speaking, intimidating and threatening us over the PA system. He talked about how they'd killed Blago Zadar. We only found out how he had been killed when we talked to people from his own unit in Borovo Naselje as well as later on in the camp. And once we had been released from the camp, we learned about the details of what exactly had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just another question about this. You mentioned the name of a person who you say had hosted Seselj at the time. Where was this person's house located inside Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Svetozar Markovic Street which is just off Radnicka Street. That was the street -- that was the name of street before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the north of Vukovar, or the south of Vukovar, the east of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a district known from before World War II as the German hill. That's where you can find both Svetozar Markovic and Radnicka streets, because up to World War II most of the people living there were Germans.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume that during the war this district of Vukovar was not under the control of the Croatian forces. Would I be right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. It wasn't. The barracks was nearby. And given all the weapons that our defenders had, they had to move further away. The front line ran along Sajmiste and then the street known as Duga Street, its name used to be Otokara Kersovanija Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us about the front line that ran along Sajmiste. Was this line established already in the first days of the conflict, and did this line not remain as a front line and a confrontation line for quite a long time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started somewhere around Radnicka Street, and if you bear in mind what sort of weapons our defenders had at the time, they were compelled to withdraw to Otokara Kersovanija Street. Unfortunately, as the defenders were leaving this area, those civilians who stayed behind in their houses were, as a rule, killed. Great crimes were committed in this area, because people were killed indiscriminately regardless of their age.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that the only time this line was moved was on the 3rd or 4th of November; do you remember that? And was this the first time that the front line was moved or shifted from the start of the clashes onwards?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been 15 years since, and it's very difficult for me to say anything specific about the exact date. But as far as Otokara Kersovanija Street is concerned, it was about 10 days later that our defenders had to retreat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When the withdrawal took place, what was the next front line to be established? Was it somewhere near the Eltz palace?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This defence line remained for quite a long time. All the way up until the 1st of November, roughly speaking. Many attempts were made to break through this line by tanks and various routes were used down Sajmiste, the JNA was pushed back several times. And then there is another street which used to be called Three Roses and now it's called Green Street. There was several attacks there, tank attacks, from the Vuteks direction. That street is called Proleterska Street. It was during one of these attempts to penetrate closer towards the centre of town that the JNA sustained huge losses because our defenders managed to destroy a great deal of tanks. They never tried using that route again in order to reach the town centre. The next street is Svetozar Markovic Street. They tried several times down that street, but our defenders held out until the 1st of November and they were successful in pushing back any attacks that came their way. However, it wasn't because of any lack of goodwill on the part of the defenders, but they couldn't hold out any longer. They simply ran out of hand-held rocket launchers at one point, which is what they used against the tanks, in order to defend against the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking of this, do you perhaps know if the defenders took any prisoners, any prisoners from the ranks of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I heard from the defenders is that they had captured a very small number of people. Most of those captured were not really captured, but were persons who had been injured or wounded. Regardless of the fact these people were the aggressors, our defenders took these people to the hospital to be treated. It is with pride that I can thank our defenders for being so humane. They found some wounded persons and they took them to the hospital. I think anyone who worked at the hospital at the time can confirm this, that there were a great deal of attackers there who were receiving treatment, despite everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you hear of any cases where prisoners were killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I have not heard of a single such case. If I knew anything about this, I certainly wouldn't hesitate to say so. My objective is to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. If I fail to tell the truth about something that I'm aware of, I feel that that would be a great sin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about this other line following that withdrawal. How long did that remain? Did it not remain until the very last days when you say you withdrew yourself and spent that last night in the premises of your company, Elektradistribucija?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The last night between the 18th and the 19th I spent in the cellar of my -- of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The line had been abandoned in its entirety by this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 18th is usually taken to be the day that Vukovar fell. The entire city, with the exception of Borovo Naselje, was no longer being defended. That was why we spent the last night in the company building, which is about 50 metres away from the hospital. The next morning, the morning of the 19th, we tried to all reach the hospital compound because we expected that some sort of a humane exchange would take place, and that we would be allowed to go back to Croatian free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talk about exchange -- you spoke about that yesterday. You said you were expecting an exchange to take place. What sort of an exchange did you have in mind? Who was being exchanged for whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a personal answer about who I had in mind. The last day that I spent at the hospital and for several days before that when I visited some of the wounded whom I had helped ferry to the hospital, our defenders, I saw one of Seselj's men. This person had been seriously wounded, and he was staying in the same cellar with the wounded defenders of Vukovar. I reckon that because this man was there they would decide to let all the civilians go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say you spent that night before you went to the hospital, and then you say the next day "we" went. Who exactly do you mean? Was your son with you too, or did he head off in a different direction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my son and a rather large group of people over those last days they were running out of weapons and ammunition and they had nothing to defend with. The defenders attempted a break-through. I personally tried to talk both my son and the rest of the defenders into attempting a break-through, because I had had a premonition of what would befall them. Those who made the attempt for the most part survived. Those who opted to stay behind, regrettably, are still missing. Most of them at least. The fate of at least 500 defenders remains unknown to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your son was one of those who attempted a break-through and he made it. He must have told you whether there was any combat along the way? I'm referring to him and the group that he was with, how they eventually reached Croatian territory. Did they have to fight their way through or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this break-through attempt they passed near the aggressors and near tanks several times. They were attacked several times. And as they were taking their escape they had to swim across the Vuka three times, and this was a cold winter month already. They had to swim across, back and forth several times. I imagine it must have been very difficult for them. There was this group with my son, and they strayed into a minefield. He was wounded. It wasn't a large wound, thank God, so they succeeded in breaking through, this group that he was with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see or hear that certain defenders would come to the hospital, leave their uniforms there, or any weapons they had, in order to change into civilians clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that, but not in or near the hospital. It was further off, near Kiviceva [phoen] Street. The defenders were left without weapons or any means of defending. They all left a bomb or several bullets for the last, and whenever I talked to them, they said, This is just in case I'm captured. I will not allow them to kill me and torture me. This was an area where most of them discarded whatever uniforms they had, and whatever weapons they had. Leaving a single hand-grenade for the very last in the event they were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After the war did you perhaps hear that after this the JNA even found storages where weapons were being stored in Vukovar, that there were such things around town?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard about anything like that at all. But caches of weapons, I don't know. Perhaps there were weapons, but there was certainly no ammunition and what use would the weapons have been then? Maybe they found that sort of a cache or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said a while ago that you personally saw people discarding whatever weapons they still carried. You mentioned hand-grenades too. Where were they discarding these things?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it was on Kiviceva Street, behind those houses facing the Vuka. There is a sandy area there, no buildings, it's an open area, and that's where they discarded most of the things that they were still carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see where they went from there, wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best part of them attempted this break-through and very few of them reached the hospital. Unfortunately, those who stayed came to grief for the most part. They were killed. I can tell you specifically about two young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please stick to my question and what I'm asking you, just in order to be as brief as possible? Your answer seems to imply that most of those who were discarding their weapons later joined the break-through attempt. Did they go just like that, without any weapons? Don't you think you might be slightly off the mark by claiming this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who stayed, yes. Those people were discarding their weapons. And those who joined the break-through, each brought a hand-grenade, perhaps a rifle with several bullets level in it. They were all saying the same thing: Should we be captured, we would rather just end our own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But my previous question was about those who stayed, who changed into civilian clothes and discarded their weapons. Did you see where those people went? More specifically, did they also go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some at the hospital, but that was a minority, I believe. Because the defenders too had their families, their parents, their grandparents. They would go to see them for the most part, to look after them, to try to save them. Most of the civilians, as you know, were staying in cellars all over town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about the night you spent at Elektradistribucija. You talked to your work-mates and you tried to persuade them to go to the hospital with you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also went on to say that you were exceptionally pleased that you had succeeded in persuading them to join you on your way to the hospital. Can you explain this? Can you tell us why you were pleased?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. And I am still pleased about this. I was expecting that everybody who was inside the hospital compound would receive better treatment, in a way. For the most part the people assembled there were women, children, not babies but primarily school-aged children. And I was assuming that the aggressors would allow all the people assembled there to leave and go back to free Croatian territory. That is why I went several times back and forth between the hospital and my company. I tried to persuade people, this took some time, but eventually I managed to talk everyone into going to the hospital, which they all did, finally. By this time there were a great many people inside the hospital compound from a variety of different buildings in the neighbourhood, civilians who had taken shelter in these cellars. As I said yesterday, there were at least 2.000 civilians in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you have just described, if I understood you correctly, on the morning of the 19th you reached the hospital and then you went back and forth several times between the hospital and Elektradistribucija trying to talk your work-mate, your colleagues into joining you at the hospital. Did you talk to any of the hospital management at any time? You did say that you had met Vesna Bosanac on one occasion. Was that later on or on that same day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally meet Vesna Bosanac. You probably misunderstood something I said. Our own manager, the company manager, met with Vesna Bosanac and talked to her. So I spoke to him to ask him whether Dr. Bosanac had told him anything, given the fact that she had been involved in negotiations with the attackers, anything about our chances of being allowed to go back to Croatia. But I never spoke to Vesna Bosanac personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I probably misunderstood something you said yesterday. You were probably told something by this person that you mentioned and what did this person tell you, exactly? Who did he meet and what was he told?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that what the doctor had told him was not very good news. He was still hopeful, however, that she would manage to broker some sort of agreement for all those inside the hospital compound to be allowed to leave and go to Vinkovski and onwards from there. I regret to say that this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume you know who Marin Vidic, Bili, was. Did you see him at the hospital, or did you hear perhaps that he was at the hospital at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Marin Vidic, Bili, I didn't see him. Look, it's been 15 years since and it's difficult for me to remember. That's one thing. The other thing is, there was a huge crowd of civilians there. Most of them were elderly, and women. It was dark, and it's really difficult to say. You could only see those who were standing close to you. As I explained yesterday, I saw the son of my wife's uncle, Stjepan Petrovic, and he ended up at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about leaving the hospital on trucks that were lined up there for you, can you describe these trucks, please? Did it have the tarp, tarpaulin, did it have any seats inside? You said that in your estimate it was big enough to hold as many as 25 people, and you said that there were twice as many of you there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a military truck and since I was a reserve officer, I was familiar with the looks of such a military truck. And I knew that there would be benches for sitting on along the sides under normal conditions, but these trucks had no benches, whatsoever. Younger people who could climb on to it, and I myself was basically letting the lorry drag me along and managed to clamber in. But something that stuck in my memory and something that I still feel very sorry about, elderly women who couldn't move easily were being thrown onto these trucks like sacks of potatoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said this yesterday, so let's not repeat things here. We need to speed things up. So may I appeal to you once again to simply keep your answers as brief as possible and answer my questions. You said there with were no benches. Was there a tarpaulin?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, but there were no benches.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that a tarpaulin which was covering that part of the truck?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it covered the truck on top and along the sides. As usual, only the back was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say the back was open, does it mean that the tarpaulin could have been moved or there was no tarpaulin at all at the back of the truck?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't noticed it, but at any rate it was not closed. And precisely because of that, as we were being driven to Vupik and Velepromet, we could see dead bodies in the streets. That's what I said yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where exactly were you in that truck?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to be in the back, in fact. And I had the opportunity to see and when we crossed Vuka I saw a colleague of mine, somebody who used to work with me, Zvonimir Vilner was his name, he was lying dead in the street. I could realise -- I could tell that he was one of us because of his jacket, because we had those jackets at the company. Everybody -- all the employees had those jackets, so that's how I recognised him from afar. And then I took a closer look and I recognised Zvonimir Vilner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you recognised the person lying in the street, or rather the dead body lying in the street. As you drove by, you were looking out from the truck and that's how you could recognise Zvonimir Vilner's dead body, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us that either at that time or before there was no street -- there was no electricity in the streets, there were no lights in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it possible that you could see and not just see, but even recognise somebody lying in the street peering out from the back of a truck? Do you think that's possible?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainly possible, plus there was moonlight, and since we had spent many years working together as colleagues, it didn't take much for me to recognise him. I saw his face. My attention was drawn to this jacket I mentioned before. I knew it must have been one of our staff. And then I -- we came closer and I could see the shape of his head and we had spent ages working together. I was certain it was him. And unfortunately when I came back from the camp, I heard the news that it had indeed been him, and unfortunately his brother got killed as well, and their mother died soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There is a mistake maybe in the transcript. I think you said "I didn't have to look at his face." Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to, because he spent many years working with me, and I believe that it is very easy for me to have recognised his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you because there seems to be a mistake in the transcript according to which you have said "I saw his face." And I think you said "I didn't need to look at his face in order to recognise him." Is the conclusion now that you could assume that was this person on the basis of his jacket, or did you reach that conclusion later on when you heard that he had actually been killed on that spot?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were passing by on the basis of the jacket, I knew it was a member of our staff. And I said that I thought it was Zvonimir Vilner, but I can say that at that moment I wasn't 100 per cent sure. But when I came back from the camp and when I talked to other people about our staff, it was confirmed, and then I said I myself saw him as well, but at that first instant I wasn't 100 per cent certain, because it was at night, even though there was moonlight, and obviously one could not make such claims 100 per cent. But 90 per cent I was sure. I was sure it was him. And then I received confirmation, and it turned out I was right when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave that topic now. You first got to Vupik on that truck. Is that so? Could you tell us roughly how long did you spend there before you went on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there for a very short time, not more than half an hour, I believe. Because we were separated straight away, men were separated from women, children and the very old, and it took a very short time, and then a group of us, about 50 of us were separated from the rest, and on the basis of an order from an officer, we were taken to Velepromet. It could have taken 30 minutes at most, according to my assessment, perhaps even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if my understanding is correct, it was there at Vupik that you, 50 men, were separated in a group and placed in another truck. Perhaps you had all gotten off the other trucks that you were on before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you must have misunderstood. I'm not talking about a truck here, we were just separated from the other people. And we were in a group, in a column, two by two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So 50-something of you were taken to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all ordered to go there. There was just a difference between that separate group of us and the others, because the others were shut into hangars straight away, and about 50 of us were lined up in front of the hangars, and throughout the time until we left for the camp, we were there about two metres away from the hangars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, we're talking only about this group of 50 men. Did you know anyone of them in person? Could you tell us who else was with you or were the other people totally unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people I knew by sight, and it was at night, and out of fear we didn't actually look that hard. There was Mr. Terek who was a neighbour of mine, and he was standing pretty close to me, so he was the only person I actually knew. And there were many other people I knew by sight, but I wasn't really interested in their names at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So apart from this gentleman called Terek, you didn't know anyone else's name, and you can't say anything much about them. Now, I would like to show you a photo. Could you tell me whether you can recognise Velepromet on this photo?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could we show the picture that we received from the Prosecution, RN 0467-2115.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the Velepromet company. And you can see clearly where the hangars were, where most people were locked up. And this is where we were, right in front of this building in the middle, and about 50 of us were standing in front of those hangars. And that's when events that I talked about yesterday took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could we blow up this picture a little bit? And the usher can help you out, and he'll give you a pencil. Can you mark the place where you were with this group of 50 people? Could you place an A there, a capital A? And encircle that letter A.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this is where you were. This group of 50-something people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I drew a line along where we were. I remember that clearly, and since every year we honour the memory of that day, and we visit the site, it sticks in my memory. I can remember it very well, indeed. If I may just add, on the other side, in the middle of this picture, and on the other side there was also a large number of civilians who had been brought there, but whom we could not see at the time, but we found out later that there was a large group of civilians on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you drew a line, what does it mean? Is it a column or were you standing in a column about 50 of you, and that's why you drew a line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your understanding is correct. This why I drew a straight line, because about 50 of us were standing, we were lined up in front of those hangars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please mark with a letter A the spot where you personally were standing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself was standing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You marked a circle there. Could you just put a letter A somewhere next to it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned in the course of examination-in-chief that the others were in the hangars. Could you mark the hangars -- is it the hangars that are just behind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the hangars which are behind us in a row, and they're huge. And very many civilians were cramped there. You could hardly stand inside. So that's how it was. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with a letter B?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you were an eye-witness to murder there, a person called Kemo was killed. Is that correct? Could you mark the place where this Kemo person and the two Chetniks that you mentioned as his killers were standing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want another letter to indicate that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, C.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here. In front of where I was standing. About two metres in front of me. This boy who was slaughtered. I did not know him, and I was surprised, because a civilian said this is Kemo, Ustasha, and -- well, I don't need to go into all this. If you want to know anything more, you can ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have also told us that occasionally you heard stifled shots every now and then. Could you tell us from what direction? Could you mark it with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That shooting came from here. I can draw a line there. First of all, I'll draw a circle. This is the brickworks here, and that's where the shooting was. And it went from there -- I mean, people were taken to that hole in the brickworks and they were shot there. Since it was a little bit further away from the hangars, we could still hear the shots, and they were being killed. But the shots we heard were not the normal sound. They were stifled. And there were -- they had silencers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We're going to move on a little bit and then I'll come back to this. Could you please mark this with a D?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. If I need to explain a little bit more, since my sister's son, my nephew --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You did mention that yesterday. Perhaps I will ask about this, but if I may, I would just like to finish up on this one. So you've marked this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask for this picture and the relevant markings to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we have been in session about an hour and a quarter, and given the circumstances of the witness, I think we might have a further break now, if that's a convenient time for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at five minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --- Break taken at 4.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Covic, earlier on when we were looking at that picture you marked several spots there. And you told us that you visited that place several times; every year, in fact. And you must be in a position to assess the length of one of these hangars. I believe they're all the same size. So how long, how deep it would be?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe 15 to 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You don't think it's much more than that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. It isn't. I was there. Certainly 15 metres, possibly 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said yesterday in reply to some of the questions, the only killing that you were an actual eye-witness to was the killing of that man called Kemo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that after that his dead body was dragged away. Where was it dragged to? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dragged to the right of where we were standing in front of the hangars that we saw on that picture. So on the inner side of the Velepromet complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You showed us on this picture today, you actually drew a straight line where some 50 of you were standing in a column, one by one, and then you also explained that you were taken there, you walked in twos from Vupik, and apart from Mr. Parek [as interpreted], you did not know anyone else and you didn't actually have time to think about it or see it. The reason I'm asking is this: Yesterday in answer to a question put to you by my learned colleague, about whether half of those people, 25 people who were separated from you on that occasion, whether you saw any of them after the war and were you answer was no. And my question is this: Would it be possible, according to what you've told us today, that you would actually be in a position to identify these people since you didn't know their names and their surnames and a long time has passed, so could they really be etched in your memory? I'm wondering about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an inaccuracy in the beginning of your question. The passage from Vupik to Velepromet, well, I didn't say we were walking in twos holding hands or anything. I mean, I said that we were walking in twos as we were marched to the buses and taken to the camps afterwards, and here we just moved as a group following orders. So you misunderstood me on that one. And those 50 of us who were there, well, more than half, certainly, according to my assessment, I mean, when we were ordered to move to the buses to be taken to the camps, I believe that about 20 people were left, and those people who were standing in a column were being taken behind the hangars, and we could see shots being -- we could hear, sorry, shots being fired. So on that basis I can conclude that all of them had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you will agree that it's just an assumption on your part, because you were not an eye-witness to those killings and you wouldn't be able to identify those people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to identify them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As to this Kemo, you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question that was asked specifically was whether in actual fact, because of the passage of time, whether the witness would be able to identify them. And that was -- that was the nature of the question. The answer actually wasn't specifically dealt with. I don't know whether the witness actually understood what the question was, or partially understood it, but in fairness to him, surely he should have the question put again to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say so, this wasn't my question about the passage of time and all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that goes back to the earlier question, Mr. Domazet. The question rather grew along. But your precise question is at -- "it's just an assumption on your part, because you were not an eye-witness to those killings, and you wouldn't be able to identify those people." The answer is: "I wouldn't be able to identify them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but with the utmost respect, that is capable of two constructions. One, I would not be able to identify them vis-a-vis at the time; or the ones who had been killed, I would be in a position either not to identify or to identify the people who had been killed. And it's capable of a double construction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I was about to go on to say that the question has two very distinct limbs. Just your last question. And you've got an answer dealing with one of them. As Mr. Moore has just pointed out, that answer, what is meant by it, is unclear. But you haven't got any answer at all to the first limb of it. So at the moment, if you want to clarify it, do so. If you're happy with the answer you've got, you can leave it. Just be aware that it may be something that you see as very important, and I think the answer you've got is not terribly satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try so as to avoid any misunderstandings. Now, my question was about the passage of time. Mr. Covic, in spite of this passage of time, seems to have a fairly good recollection of have a fairly good recollection of events if we look at the testimony and we think back of his testimony in the course of yesterday and today. But the question put by my learned colleague Moore was put in a different way, that is to say, those people who were taken away, whether he of encountered them or met them after the war. And my question is, would he have been able to identify these people, would he have had the opportunity to remember their faces in order for him to be able to recognise them in any given situation afterwards, so I am going to repeat this once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Covic, clarify that now? Apart from Mr. Terek, did you know any of them, and would you be able to recognise them on the basis of their names and surnames or recognise their faces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Terek was standing next to me, and together with him, well, we held hands when this JNA major issued the order to do so when we were sent to these camps, and he's still alive. He is not missing or anything. Because the ones who were taken away, I mean, it was at night, so it was a bit difficult to recognise everything. I saw that they were being taken to the brickworks, and obviously today I wouldn't be able to identify their bodies if I were asked to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm not talking about dead bodies. What I want to know is whether you would be able to identify these persons. Did you know their names, so that several years later, or much later, you could identify these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did say that I -- I didn't know their names. I knew many of them by sight. Vukovar is not such a small place after all, and many people were brought there from different parts of town. It was impossible to know everyone there. You might have known some people, people who worked with you, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not dwell on this any longer. I do have to ask you one thing: This man named Terek who you say survived, what is his name exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terek is his last name, and I can't remember what his first name was. We called him Terek. I knew his wife slightly better. She was a saleswoman, but I don't think that is a very crucial matter, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: A while ago when you marked that spot where you saw this person you identified as Kemo, you heard this person's name was Kemo, I think you said his body was identified by a young man, but yesterday you said it was a lady who pointed him out and that was why he was taken to one side. Now, which is true? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. But if I look at the way your question is phrased, I believe you misunderstood my original answer to that question. What I said yesterday is that among those civilians passing our group, I only recognised three. I even know their names: Mile Macesic; another man, nicknamed Kesega, the son of Miro Stankovic, the former manager or director of the Vukovar newspapers and radio; and there was a young lady I recognised too. I didn't know what her name was, and I still don't know. I know she worked with the Committee of the League of Communists. As for those three, I didn't say that they pointed out this young man who was killed. But there were other local civilians passing by. Among them was someone, I'm not sure who exactly who pointed the young man out. And Mile Macesic was the man who pointed out me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You have clarified the matter sufficiently. It appears that my understanding was wrong, but it's fine now. You did not know this person named Kemo. Do you perhaps know the man's last name, and could it be Saiti?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know this young man at all. I expected Kemo to be some sort of a nickname. There was this person who pointed their finger at him, and I didn't know his name, not then, not now. I simply figured that this was a nickname that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember when giving your statement to the OTP investigators handing over a list of persons you defined as local Chetniks or local Serbs who committed crimes and who you were able to identify or someone who was helping you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a list that I submitted. I just enumerated a number of persons I recognised back at the hospital and in the Velepromet area. Those were the names that I gave during the interview. But it was not a list, as such. No substantial list. It was probably provided by someone else, another witness. And whoever drew up that particular list must have known what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It might be an error there because we have received a list with 51 names on it that was attached to your statement. My assumption was that you produced this list, but Mile Macesic is not on it, or the other man named Fot?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So I was wondering why these two names missing and you keep referring to them. But if you were not the person who produced this list, then I can only offer my sincere apologies and move on in a different direction with my questions. I am about to complete my cross-examination, but I would like to ask the Court to please briefly go into private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Covic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
